title: Social Media API Design
description: Design a social media API for posts, comments, follows, and feeds with efficient pagination and relationship modeling.

data.text: Social media APIs have unique challenges: high-volume writes, complex relationships (follows, likes, blocks), and feeds that must scale to millions of users. You need a resource model that supports both public and private interactions.

data.title: Core resources
items: Posts — text, image, or video content authored by a user
Follows — directed edge from follower to followee
Likes — reactions on posts or comments
Feeds — personalized timelines derived from follows

data.text: Feeds can contain millions of items. Offset pagination breaks when new posts arrive during pagination. Use cursor-based pagination with a stable, monotonic sort key (created_at or Snowflake ID).

rows: Breaks on concurrent inserts, slow on large offsets
Stable under concurrent inserts, fast deep pagination
No random access, requires sort key

data.title: GET /users/{id}/feed?limit=20&cursor=eyJpZCI6MTIzNX0
data.content: Cursor pagination uses opaque base64-encoded cursors containing the last item's sort key.

data.text: The follow relationship is a directed edge. Store it in a graph-optimized store or a relational junction table. Index both (follower_id, followee_id) and (followee_id, follower_id) for bidirectional lookups.

data.title: Feed fan-out patterns
data.text: Use push fan-out (write to all followers' timelines at post creation) for regular users with <10K followers. Use pull fan-out (query follows on read) for celebrities with millions of followers.

data.title: POST /posts
data.content: Creating a post triggers async fan-out to followers' timelines.

items.question: How do I handle blocked users in feeds?
items.answer: Maintain a block list per user. Before inserting a post into a user's feed, check if the post author is blocked. Push fan-out should skip blocked relationships.

items.question: Should I use GraphQL instead of REST for feeds?
items.answer: GraphQL works well for mobile clients that need variable field selection. REST with cursor pagination is simpler to operate and cache at the edge. Many social platforms offer both.

items.question: How do I prevent duplicate posts in a feed?
items.answer: Use the post ID as a unique key in the timeline cache. Before inserting, check if the ID already exists. Idempotent writes prevent duplicate fan-out on retries.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Cursor pagination is essential for stable feeds under concurrent writes.
Use push fan-out for normal users and pull for celebrities.
Treat relationships as first-class resources with their own endpoints.
Visibility and block lists must be enforced at write time, not read time.
data.takeaway: Social APIs are write-heavy and relationship-driven. Design for fan-out scale from the start, or you will rebuild your feed infrastructure twice.
